outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Procedural Background and the Parties' Claims
outline.description: Sets the factual and procedural foundation of the case, introducing the agencies, statutes, and the litigation history that led to the appellate review.
subtopics: The Office of Special Counsel (OSC): statutory mandate and enforcement powers under the Civil Service Reform Act
Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and its specific enforcement provision (552(a)(4)(F)(i))
America First Legal Foundation’s (AFL) FOIA request to the DOJ and the DOJ’s partial compliance
AFL’s request for OSC to investigate alleged illegal FOIA policy under 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3)
OSC’s refusal to investigate and the district court’s partial‑grant, partial‑dismiss outcome
Procedural posture: district court’s remand, second refusal, entry of judgment, and appeal to the D.C. Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Governing Law – Standing Doctrine and the Limits of Procedural Rights
outline.description: Explains the constitutional and doctrinal framework governing Article III standing, emphasizing the elements of injury, causation, and redressability, and clarifies the distinction between substantive and procedural injuries.
subtopics: Article III case‑or‑controversy requirement and the Lujan test (injury, causation, redressability)
Standard for pleading standing at the motion‑to‑dismiss stage (Food & Water Watch)
Procedural‑injury standing: relaxed standards and their limits (Center for Law & Education v. Dep’t of Educ.; Summers v. Earth Island Inst.)
The “procedural right in vacuo” principle and its relevance to statutory rights without a concrete interest
The informational‑standing doctrine (AFL v. Feld; Zivotofsky; Akins) and why it matters here

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: AFL’s Two Standing Theories and the Court’s Analysis
outline.description: Breaks down each of AFL’s alleged injuries, the court’s application of standing principles, and why each theory fails.
subtopics: First theory: injury from DOJ’s alleged failure to produce FOIA records
Causation analysis – speculative chain involving OSC, MSPB, and DOJ
Redressability analysis – why a judgment would not bind the non‑parties
Second theory: informational injury from the lack of OSC investigation and notices
Entitlement analysis – statutory language of § 1216(a)(3) vs. § 1214 procedural guarantees
Discretionary nature of OSC’s investigative decision‑making (Heckler v. Chaney)
Court’s conclusion that AFL lacks a concrete injury under both theories

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: The Holding, Disposition, and Its Implications
outline.description: Summarizes the appellate court’s final conclusion, the procedural result, and the broader significance for standing and OSC enforcement.
subtopics: Holding: AFL lacks Article III standing; district court judgment vacated
Remand instructions – dismissal for lack of subject‑matter jurisdiction
Implications for future challenges to OSC discretion under § 1216
Effect on litigants seeking procedural enforcement of FOIA policies
Key takeaway: statutory procedural rights do not create Article III jurisdiction absent concrete injury
